title: Trinidadian Pelau
subtitle: Trinidadian one-pot caramelised chicken and rice with coconut milk
excerpt: Pelau is a Trinidadian one-pot dish where chicken is browned in caramelised sugar before being cooked with rice, coconut milk, and vegetables. The burnt sugar gives a dark, slightly bitter note that balances the sweetness of the coconut. It is Sunday cooking in Trinidad.
sourceNotes: Pelau has roots in the pilaf traditions brought to the Caribbean by Spanish colonisers from the Moorish-influenced cooking of Andalusia, and was further shaped by African and Indian influences. The use of browning -- burning sugar to colour the chicken -- is distinctly Trinidadian.

content.text: The browning step -- caramelising sugar until dark and slightly bitter -- is the heart of pelau. Do not stop too early or the colour and flavour will not develop. The sugar should be a very dark amber before the chicken goes in. Have everything else ready before you start this step.

items.prepNote: use a 400ml tin of coconut milk

content.text: Heat the oil and brown sugar in a large heavy pot over medium heat. Cook without stirring until the sugar melts and turns a very dark amber -- almost black. This takes 3 to 4 minutes.
Add the chicken pieces immediately. They will spit -- stand back. Toss to coat in the caramel. Brown for 5 minutes.
Add the onion, garlic, thyme, and allspice. Cook for 3 minutes.
Add the carrots. Pour in the coconut milk and 400ml of water. Season with salt. Bring to the boil.
Add the rinsed rice. Stir once. Reduce to the lowest heat possible. Cover tightly and cook for 20 minutes.
Add the peas and green beans. Cover again for 5 minutes. Rest off the heat for 5 minutes before opening. Serve from the pot.

items.symptom: Sugar burnt to ash rather than dark caramel
items.fix: Use medium heat and watch it closely -- you want very dark amber, not black and smoking

items.symptom: Rice is still wet at the bottom
items.cause: Too much liquid or lid not tight
items.fix: Seal the lid with foil under it if your lid does not fit tightly; cook for 5 more minutes

items.cause: Sugar was allowed to burn too far
items.fix: The caramel needs to be dark amber -- stop before it smokes or turns black

content.text: Pelau is Trinidad's version of a pilaf -- cooked in one pot with everything together. It is the quintessential Sunday lunch in Trinidad, eaten at family gatherings and cricket matches. The burnt sugar browning technique, called burning the sugar, is the signature step that makes it Trinidadian rather than anything else.
